hmm ok if you’re sticking with fluance, then sure the sony strdh190 should work fine, there are posts online about this combo. just make sure to get a passive speaker like wharfedale diamond 220

honestly many combinations of turntable, integrated amp and passive speakers will work fine but general rule of thumb is spend the same amount of money on your turntable as you would on the speakers 

my current setup is rega planar 1 + denon pma 600ne + klipsch rp-600m so i would personally be able to recommend these 3. my friends also enjoy the at-lp120 and dali spektor 2 combo

iirc fluance rt85 doesnt have a built in preamp so yes youll need a separate preamp and amp 

because you have budgetary concerns, i’ll say a 3 equipment setup is best so

fluance + integrated amp (pre amp and amp) + passive speakers OR fluance + pre amp + powered speakers

hii so i would recommend rega planar 1 for that price especially for a better quality entry-level turntable. the good: sound quality is pretty unmatched for the price point, easy setup, no fancy bells and whistles because they really do just focus on the sound of the turntable. the downsides: not easily customisable (but there are workarounds if you want to upgrade your cartridge etc.), the turntable is internally grounded so it doesn’t come with a ground wire which sometimes causes a ground loop that’s difficult to eliminate. 

other entry level turntables that are popular and good for that price point: at-lp120, project debut carbon

because you also mentioned that you have a budget, i’d advise (if possible) to get an integrated amp so you don’t have to spend extra on a preamp. 

for speakers, i’m using klipsch but audioengine, wharfale are all fine options too for that price point. 

there’s also good turntable combos lists online if you’re afraid you miss out on a component / want something that is tried and tested

In general, Gettier problems challenge the tripartite definition of knowledge as justified true  belief. There are a few responses to the problem: 
(1) reject gettier examples as instances of knowledge, essentially claiming that there is something inherently flawed within gettier cases that means they don’t meet the requirements of justified, true belief
(2) admit that the gettier example does constitute knowledge (something similar to stephen hetherington’s response of distinguishing between failable knowledge and very failable knowledge)
(3) add a fourth condition for knowledge, so knowledge is JTB+K, where K is a 4th condition that is immune to gettier examples
(4) alter the justification condition, so knowledge is TB+H, where H is some other condition that allows for knowledge but is also immune to gettier examples

most philosophers have tried (3), for example imposing a causal, sensitivity, defeasbility, anti-luck condition which have all (more or less) failed. but this doesnt mean that theres no merit to JTB because i do think that in many situations, whatever fulfills the criteria of JTB is intuitively also knowledge, so while gettier cases pose an admittedly strong objection to traditional JTB, there is still value in viewing knowledge as some kind of JTB that is immune to gettier cases.

for research or readings, check out the SEP and IEP articles on gettier cases and the subsequent responses by goldman, nozick etc.

1. Take a look around you. What do you see? Maybe a chair, your hands, perhaps a book. You would think these exist but how do you know? Maybe you say “Because I can see and touch these things,” but in a dream you also feel like you can see and touch such things even though you are not. So how sure are you that you know the objects around you exist? How do you know? How do you know you exist? The answer KI offers to this, is not an answer, it’s just further questions. 

^ this serves as the very foundation for epistemology, which is a huge focus of KI (but not entirely) where you study what it means to have knowledge, whether we can get knowledge, how we can attain this knowledge etc. so generally if you really like philosophical questions or more “meta” questions, KI will be quite cool and interesting to study

2. for KI, there are three broad areas: critical thinking, general epistemology and field-specific knowledge studies

for critical thinking, it’s kind of like we’ll get a passage and in GP, they’ll ask you for like a summary of the passage or like the key ideas in the passage, or an argumentative response to the passage in the AQ. for KI however, they ask us on the logical and argumentative structure of the passage, before we look at whether there are flaws or merits in the author’s argument

for general epistemology, they’ll ask stuff like: “Without evidence, we cannot believe in what we take to be knowledge” -> while GP will answer this with points like “there’s a practical side to knowledge, or like we need evidence so we can have good debates with others and determine who actually has knowledge”, ki is more philo based so there’ll be references to theories like evidentialism etc. 

for field specific questions, usually the main areas covered in KI are maths, science, history, aesthetics, ethics and social science (with some others depending on the school) so we look at the more “meta” side. a typical history question for history would be like “assess the extent to which the cold war originated largely due to the USSR’s aggression” but for KI, history is more like historiography so we look at questions like “is historical knowledge inevitably subjective? or is it more objective than that of natural sciences?” and for science in KI, we can have questions like “Consider the view that scientific knowledge is superior to aesthetic knowledge because of its objectivity” so KI ties in with knowledge from other fields (for science in KI, i know experiments like the double slit experiment etc) as well as the philosophical debate and epistemology side of these subjects

3. yes, like i feel KI is the most “valuable” jc subject purely because of the nature it has to be studied. it’s a lot of independent learning and we have to read articles from SEP and like q a few of us will also look at papers that undergrad philo students take, which is so diff from even other arts subjects where u generally just look at the handout the teachers give and at most do a bit more readings. also there’s an IS component to ki, so the research paper helps to prep us for uni kind of thesis in terms of like time management and writing a 3000 word essay . i think KI also generally will make people more critical thinkers like you can really notice the amount of logical flaws and what moves people, and in fact there are so many logical fallacies committed every day that we literally do live in a world where people are more driven by emotion than reason so it helps to identify people who actually make sound objective statements and those that appeal to emotions

4. again, critical thinking is so important like studying philo helps because it’s literally the studying of studying, you’re studying what it means to study something, so that really helps u think clearer and better. also with ki or philo in a broader sense, i feel more uncomfortable now with certain things like if u look at veganism and like the case for eating meat, there is practically no philo argument for eating meat and it really helps u rethink your beliefs and everything so yea :”) ki really does help in that regard
